guideTitle: Best Leaf Blowers for Large Yards (2026)
metaTitle: Best Leaf Blowers for Large Yards in 2026
metaDescription: Six backpack and cordless leaf blowers for half-acre to multi-acre lots, compared by engine size, battery runtime, volume and carry comfort.
expertTake: The Husqvarna 360BT is the best blower for a large yard because it combines 890 CFM, a 65.6cc engine and a harness built for hour-long sessions. The PROYAMA 72cc is the value pick if you accept thinner dealer support. Skip handheld cordless blowers on lots over an acre unless you own several spare batteries, because the runtime math simply does not work.
introParagraphs: On a large yard the limiting factor is not peak airflow but how long you can keep working at a steady output. A blower that is fine for twenty minutes can become an hour of recharging, refuelling and sore shoulders across an acre of leaf fall.

That shifts the buying logic toward endurance: engine displacement or battery capacity, a harness that spreads weight, and a throttle that holds a setting. Volume matters more than speed, since the job is moving a lot of leaves a long distance.

products.name: Husqvarna 360BT backpack, 65.6cc, 890 CFM, 232 MPH
products.description:
On a big lot the 360BT is the machine that gets the job done without fuss. Its 65.6cc X-Torque engine is a low-emission two-stroke design that keeps output steady, and the 890 CFM volume lets you push a wide windrow of leaves down a lawn in one pass. The backpack harness is not a luxury: carrying a gas blower in your hands for an hour is what ends the session early.

Against the cheaper PROYAMA, which claims 880 CFM from a 72cc engine, the Husqvarna looks similar on paper but wins on the things the spec sheet does not show: dealer service, parts supply and a long record of the engine design. Against the ECHO PB-9010T, it gives up volume, 890 against 1110 CFM, in return for a lighter, more manageable machine.

Plan the ownership honestly. Mix premix at the maker's ratio, clean the air filter every few sessions because leaf dust clogs it, and check the spark plug each season. Before winter drain the tank and run the carburetor dry, and inspect the harness and its stitching because it takes the abuse. Adjust the hip belt so the engine rides on your pelvis, not your shoulders, and take a five minute break each fuel stop so your hands recover from the vibration.
products.bestFor: Half-acre to multi-acre lots where reliability and dealer support matter.
pros: 890 CFM and 232 MPH is a strong balance
Harness is built for long sessions
Engine design aims at steady sustained output
cons: Loud enough to need hearing protection

products.name: ECHO PB-9010T backpack, 79.9cc, 1110 CFM, 220 MPH
products.description:
The PB-9010T is the biggest blower in the guide by engine size and airflow, a 79.9cc two-stroke producing 1110 CFM. That volume is the cheat code for acreage: a wide column of air moves leaves further per pass, which cuts the number of passes across a field. The tube-mounted throttle lets you set a cruising speed with your hand on the nozzle.

It is a heavy, serious tool, and the price is paid in fuel and noise. On a half-acre it is overkill, and the Husqvarna 360BT is more comfortable. On three acres of oak and maple, the extra volume saves real time.

Treat it like a small engine you own. Use fresh premix, keep the air filter clean, torque the exterior fasteners after the first few hours, and check the throttle cable and harness each season. Stabilize or drain fuel before storage so the carburetor stays clean. On a large property a tidy habit is to keep a dedicated fuel can and funnel with the machine, so you are never tempted to top up with stale mix.
products.bestFor: Properties of two acres or more with heavy leaf loads.
pros: 1110 CFM is the highest volume here
Large engine holds output under load

products.name: PROYAMA 72cc gas backpack, 880 CFM, 275 MPH, dual nozzle
products.description:
PROYAMA gives you a larger engine than the Husqvarna, 72cc against 65.6cc, plus a dual-tube design with flat and round nozzles that adapt the jet to the job. A flat nozzle sweeps lawn in a wide band, while the round one hits stuck debris with a concentrated stream. The listing mentions low vibration and snow clearing as extra uses.

The 3.7 horsepower figure is a claim, not a rated number, and the value tier it sits in tells you where corners are cut: brand support, parts supply and long-term engine history. For a homeowner who clears leaves a few times a year, that is an acceptable trade for a lower entry cost.

Keep a spare spark plug and air filter in the shed, retorque bolts after the first few hours, and run fresh premix. Because dealers are limited, buy a service kit with it, and check the warranty terms on the listing before you commit.
products.bestFor: Large-yard owners who want gas power at a value tier and can do their own upkeep.
pros: 72cc engine with 880 CFM at a value tier
Dual nozzles for sweeping and stuck debris
275 MPH jet is the fastest gas option here
cons: Power claim is not an independent rating

products.name: EGO Power+ LB8803-2 cordless blower, 880 CFM, two 4.0Ah
products.description:
On a large lot the EGO is the battery blower worth considering because it is the only cordless model here with a 90 minute claim across two packs and 880 CFM of volume. That is competitive with the 880 CFM claimed by the gas PROYAMA, but without noise, fumes or fuel mixing. The turbo mode clears caked debris, and the platform gives you spare packs shared with the maker's mowers and trimmers.

The weakness is arithmetic. A claimed 90 minutes is at low speed, and on a two-acre lot you will probably burn through both packs, so you will need a third and a rapid charger. In steady use at mid-dial, plan on far less than the headline runtime.

Store the packs indoors at partial charge, rotate them, and keep the intake free of leaf dust. If you already own EGO tools, it is a very good fit; if not, a gas backpack costs less for the same acreage.
products.bestFor: Owners already in the EGO ecosystem with a one-acre lot and a spare pack.
pros: Packs shared across the EGO line
cons: Runtime falls short of acreage work without spares

products.name: Greenworks 80V brushless blower, 700 CFM, 2.5Ah battery

specList.label: Claim
specList.value: Compared by the maker with 27cc gas blowers

products.description:
Greenworks uses 80 volts to deliver 700 CFM from a brushless motor, which the maker positions against a 27cc gas blower. That is a fair comparison for the lighter end of gas power but not for the big backpack engines in this guide. It fits a property where you want quiet and no fuel, and a modest lot of about half an acre.

The 2.5Ah pack is small for large-yard work, which is the main limitation. Higher voltage helps the motor but does not change the energy in the pack, so expect shorter running time than the EGO's two 4.0Ah packs. A spare pack and a fast charger are a requirement, not a luxury.

Treat the batteries as the main long-term cost and keep them indoors at partial charge. The 80V platform has a range of other tools, so owners of those get value from the pack. If you do not own other 80V tools, weigh that against a plain gas backpack, which costs less and runs longer on this much ground.
products.bestFor: Half-acre yards where quiet matters and a spare pack is available.
pros: Platform works with other Greenworks tools
cons: Only a 2.5Ah pack in the kit
700 CFM trails the gas and EGO options
Runtime on big lots is short

products.name: ALSO GO 880 CFM brushless cordless, 280 MPH, 2 x 6.0Ah
products.description:
ALSO GO gives you the largest cordless battery pair here, two 6.0Ah packs, plus 880 CFM and a five-step speed dial. On paper it beats the EGO's 4.0Ah pair for runtime, which is the number that matters on a big lot, and the 280 MPH jet tackles damp leaves. The 1500W peak is a turbo figure.

What you do not get is the support behind it. There is no wider tool platform and the long-term parts supply is unproven. If the packs fail after two years, replacements may be hard to find, which turns a good-value tool into a disposable one.

Store the packs at partial charge, avoid hot garages and clear the intake. On a larger property, keep a spare charger at a second location so recharging does not stall the job.
products.bestFor: Owners who want the biggest cordless pack pair and do not need a platform.
pros: Two 6.0Ah packs are the largest here
cons: No tool platform or proven parts supply

buyingCriteria.explanation: A large yard means long sessions, and the longest-lasting power is gas. A 65.6cc Husqvarna runs until the tank is empty and refuels in a minute, while an EGO LB8803-2 claims 90 minutes at best and less at mid-dial. If you work more than an hour at a time, gas or a stack of spare batteries is the realistic answer.

On big lots you are moving a lot of leaves a long distance, so volume matters most. The ECHO at 1110 CFM and the Husqvarna at 890 CFM move wide windrows, while speed only helps with stuck debris at the edges. A very fast jet with low volume makes more passes.

Advertised horsepower on small gas engines is often gross. The 72cc PROYAMA claims 3.7HP and the 65.6cc Husqvarna 3.81HP, which tells you the horsepower numbers are not comparable. Use displacement as the sanity check and check brand support.

A backpack moves the load to your hips and is essential past thirty minutes. Look for padded shoulder straps and a hip belt, and check the machine's dry weight. A handheld blower at the same airflow will tire your wrist and shoulder in half the time.

A tube-mounted throttle like the ECHO's lets you adjust output without reaching back to the engine. Cruise lock on cordless tools holds a setting. A tool that forces you to squeeze a trigger for an hour will cramp your hand.

Gas needs premix, a funnel and a can, while cordless needs packs, a charger and a power outlet near your work area. Think about where you will refuel or recharge and how far it is from the far end of the lot. Spare packs are the biggest quality-of-life upgrade for cordless.

howWeEvaluated.title: Volume and coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared CFM from 700 on the Greenworks to 1110 on the ECHO. On acreage, volume decides how many passes a lawn takes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Carry comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet, we weighed backpack harnesses against handheld weight. Long sessions favour a harness. Throttle design also counted.

howToChoose.subheading: Gas vs Battery on Big Lots

cards.label: Gas
cards.text: The Husqvarna, ECHO and PROYAMA run until the tank is empty and refuel quickly. They are loud, need premix and demand seasonal care. They are the practical choice for a half-hour-plus session.

cards.label: Battery
cards.text: The EGO, Greenworks and ALSO GO are quiet and start instantly. Runtime is limited and turbo is brief. They suit lots up to an acre if you own spare packs.

howToChoose.note: Choose gas above an acre; choose battery for quieter neighbourhoods and shorter jobs.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Volume above 800 CFM and a way to sustain it. Heavy leaf fall needs wide passes, so choose a blower with a flat nozzle and a throttle that holds a setting. Plan on a break every hour for fuel or packs.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ECHO PB-9010T at 1110 CFM and the Husqvarna 360BT at 890 CFM are the best for heavy fall. The EGO LB8803-2 is the best cordless.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You work more than an hour per session, or want proven dealer support. The Husqvarna 360BT and ECHO PB-9010T pay back in service access.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You clear leaves a few weekends a year. The PROYAMA 72cc gives strong airflow at a lower tier.

maintenance.why: Leaf dust clogs the filter and richens the mix. A clean filter keeps gas engines running at full power.
Old mixed fuel gums the carburetor. Mix only what you will use in a month.
Stitching and buckles wear under load. A failed strap mid-job is a hazard.
Store at partial charge indoors and rotate packs. Heat and deep discharge cut life.
Two-stroke vibration loosens fasteners. A loose tube or handle is a safety issue.

faq.q: How much CFM do I need for a large yard?
faq.a: Above 800 CFM is the target for lots over half an acre, and 1000 plus helps on acreage. Volume moves leaves further per pass. Endurance matters as much as the number.

faq.q: Is gas or battery better for a large yard?
faq.a: Gas still wins on endurance, since a tank refuels in a minute. Battery models are quieter and easier to start, but need spare packs. Choose gas above an acre.
The PROYAMA is at the value tier for gas, the cordless kits in the middle and the Husqvarna and ECHO at the higher tiers. Spend for dealer support if you rely on the machine.

faq.q: How long do gas blowers last?
faq.a: A well-maintained two-stroke can last many seasons. Fresh premix, a clean filter and a drained tank for winter are the key. Poor fuel care is the main killer.

faq.q: Is a backpack blower worth it?
faq.a: Yes for sessions over thirty minutes. The harness moves weight off your arms. For short jobs a handheld is easier to store and handle.
Yes with gas models, and sensible with cordless on turbo. Long exposure to a blower engine can damage hearing. Wear ear protection and eye protection.
